12. It is further stated that in case of in absentia trial the limitation shall run from the date of knowledge of the judgment and not from the date of judgment and in the instant case it appears from the judicial record that the petitioner learnt about the judgment on 24-10-2004 and the appeal was filed on 1-11-2004 and in view of the fact of knowledge, the appeal was filed within time but the learned Sessions Judge has failed to apply his judicial mind while refusing the admission of the appeal. He further submitted that in accompanying of copy of the judgment appealed against is not mandatory but the appellate Court may dispense it for the interest of justice and refusing admission only because copy of the judgment is not accompanied with the petition of appeal is also against the law. He further stated that the learned Sessions Judge has passed the impugned judgment and order in violation of the provision of section 421 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. He further submits that in case of time barred Criminal Appeal preferred against conviction, the appellate Court for the interest of justice might have admitted the appeal for hearing the same on merit but in the instant case the learned Sessions Judge without entering into the merit of the case most arbitrarily refused to admit the appeal. He further submits that the instant case is an out and out a false and got-up case because, in the case it is alleged that the informant Abul Kalam while held captive of the accused, he was compelled to take photograph with a lady and it is further alleged that accused persons fled away from the place of occurrence and two of them were apprehended by the local people but prosecution was kept mum about the lady with whom the informant was forced to take photograph and absence of the lady from the scene makes whole prosecution a false story and for the interest of justice the appeal should have been admitted but the learned Sessions Judge has failed to consider the merit of the case and, as such, the impugned order is liable to be set aside. 

 17. The question whether an appeal is barred by limitation or not or whether he had been prevented by just and reasonable cause in filing the appeal in time is a question of facts to be decided by the relevant Court on an application of mind to the facts stated, and by reference to the records after considering the matter in the light of the attending fact and circumstances of each case and the finding needs to be judicially and not arbitrarily. 

 26. In a case of in absentia trial, limitation shall run from the date of knowledge of the judgment and not from the date of judgment and in the instant case it appears from the judicial record that the petitioner learnt about the judgment on 24-10-2004 and the appeal was filed on 1-11-2004 and in view of the fact of knowledge, the appeal was within time. But the learned Sessions Judge failed to apply his judicial mind while refusing the admission of the appeal. 

 31. The amended provision of law shall thus never be interpreted as proving a trial behind the back as of right but always deemed to be held to his knowledge after making it known to him by all possible ways which starts by affixing a notice at his residence for his information and if a trial is held in absentia but to the knowledge of the accused, the convicted person would also be knowing the date on which the judgment was delivered and would be obliged, if wishes to file an appeal, to file it within 30 days from the date of judgment as in all other cases of criminal appeal under the Limitation Act. 

 32. But in the case of a trial alleged to have been held without the knowledge of the accused and behind his back and the Limitation Act having not provided any special limitation for appeal in case of such trial in absentia, as if held ex parte by committing fraud upon the Court by suppressing notice, it would be in consonance with the principle of natural justice that in such an appeal, time would run from the date of appellant's knowledge of the judgment as in section 18 of the Limitation Act. Furthermore, extension of time shall always be available if sufficient cause is shown for delay. 

 34. This cited decision supports the view I have taken hereinbefore to the effect that for a case where neither the provision of the Criminal Procedure Code nor the Limitation Act clearly prescribed any date from which time would be counted for limitation as to appeal, 30 days time for appeal would be counted from the date of knowledge of the impugned order of conviction. 

 35. In the instant case the accused petitioner came to know about the judgment and order dated 8-7-2004 passed by the learned Magistrate, on 24-10-2004. In view of fact of knowledge, the appeal was within time but the learned Sessions Judge did not apply his judicial mind while refusing the admission of appeal. This ought to have been considered by the learned Sessions Judge, Sylhet while refusing admission of the appeal considering it to be time barred. It appears that the Court below in coming to a finding of fact that the appeal is barred by limitation, took a wrong view of the law, which therefore cannot be sustained.
